newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Rescuers race to find survivors, ski village prays.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers race to find survivors, ski village prays.

text.p: Rescuers on Monday raced against the weather to find 10 people still entombed in the rubble of an Australian ski resort, as more than 500 people gathered at a chapel here to pray for another miracle survivor.
Rescue workers were working feverishly to prepare for wet weather, fearing a downpour could send the tonnes of concrete slabs, twisted metal, dirt and trees crashing further down the hill.
As an emotional church service prayed for more survivors, the rescue operation had to be temporarily suspended for fear of more landslides or slipping debris.
"We pray in grief for lives lost and those which may hang in the balance. For those who sorrow and those who search," Anglican Reverend Harvey Sloane said.
Grieving relatives and friends of those missing, rescuers and politicians also offered thanks for ski instructor Stuart Diver's miraculous survival after 64 hours trapped in a concrete tomb.

Diver, 27, stunned the world on Saturday night when he emerged from his concrete sarcophagus deep within the debris at the Thredbo resort, 400 km (250 miles) south of Sydney, after surviving for three freezing nights.
"He wants everyone to know that he can move his toes even better than before. His spirits are good," said acting prime minister Tim Fischer.
Fischer had visited Diver in a hospital in nearby Canberra, where he was making a speedy recovery. Doctors had feared that Diver might need surgery to treat severe frostbite to his feet.
"He wants to say thanks and I want to say thanks on behalf of the prime minister and all Australians to all those who have been involved," Fischer told reporters after the service.
Outside the chapel, villagers linked arms and hugged each other, weeping. Ski instructors and ski rescue staff, who had hurried down from the snowfields for the service, were overcome with emotion.
Fischer said he was confident Thredbo, with a permanent population of barely 500, would recover from the disaster.
"It will take a long time in many ways, but the Snowy Mountains will bounce back and we'll be here to help," said Fischer, who cut short a trip to Japan to visit Thredbo.
The landslide, which hit just before midnight on Wednesday, destroyed two ski lodges at the Thredbo Alpine Village, burying 20 people. Nine bodies have been recovered from the wreckage.
But police said they feared expected wet weather could send tonnes of debris crashing further down the hill, hindering rescue operations and the chances of finding more survivors.
"All the experts tell us that it could rain on Wednesday and it will almost certainly rain and snow on Thursday," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson said.
Rescuers have cleared dirt from the top of the landslide and arranged for tarpaulins to be draped over a 40 metre (130 feet) by 80 metre (260 feet) patch of unstable dirt.
They have also honeycombed the debris with 24 metres (80 feet) of tunnels, burrowing by hand if need be to look for cavities that might hide life.
"One must hope that there are (more survivors) but obviously as time goes on, it's getting more and more difficult," fire brigade superintendent Ray Kelly told reporters.
Newspapers around the world on Monday carried the remarkable story of Diver's survival.

Diver and his wife Sally, who is still missing, were in bed when the disaster struck. Diver has told rescuers how he pressed his nose against a concrete slab above his head in order to breathe as water and mud filled his concrete tomb.
Some rescuers have said Diver tried desperately to save his wife after the landslide hit, but her fate is still unclear.
